## Herbivore Countermeasures {background-color="#1B4332"}

*Contre-mesures des herbivores*

::: {.notes}
Transition, ~5 sec. Every plant defense in the last section has a
matching herbivore counter-adaptation - this is the other side of the
arms race, and it closes the loop back to the phylloxera story: an
adapted enemy vs. a naive host is exactly what these countermeasures
are for.
:::

## 1. Specialized behavior

- **Vein-cutting / trenching**: monarch caterpillars sever the
  latex-filled veins of milkweed leaves *before* feeding downstream —
  draining the pressurized, toxic latex away from their meal first
- **Selective feeding**: choosing younger or older leaves, or
  specific tissue, based on where toxin concentration or trichome
  density is lowest
- **Timing**: some herbivores feed at night or feed briefly across
  many plants, limiting how much induced defense they trigger in any
  one spot

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. Vein-cutting is a great visual/memorable example - it's
literally a behavioral countermeasure engineered around one specific
plant defense structure (latex canals).
:::

## 2. Detoxification

- General xenobiotic-processing enzymes — **cytochrome P450s**,
  glutathione S-transferases, esterases — break toxins down into
  harmless (or less harmful) byproducts
- Swallowtail butterfly caterpillars (*Papilio* spp.) carry
  specialized P450 enzymes (CYP6B family) that specifically detoxify
  furanocoumarins from their host plants
- Some *Brassica* specialists neutralize glucosinolates by
  redirecting their breakdown toward a less-toxic product instead of
  the toxic one the plant "intends"

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. The glucosinolate example ties back to the
Brussels-sprouts/TAS2R38 story again - now from the insect's
counter-adaptation side.
:::

## 3. Sequestration

- Instead of breaking a toxin down, some herbivores **store it
  unmodified** in their own tissues
- Monarch caterpillars sequester milkweed **cardenolides** — the
  adult butterfly stays toxic/emetic to bird predators for life
- The plant's allomone (defends the plant, harms the herbivore)
  becomes the **herbivore's own allomone** against its predators —
  the exact same molecule, doing the same job, one trophic level up

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. Direct callback to Week 2's infochemical classification -
this is a clean example of a molecule's "who benefits" classification
flipping depending on which relationship you're looking at.
:::

## 4. Hijacking host metabolism

- **Gall-forming insects** manipulate the plant's own growth hormones
  (cytokinins, auxins) to build a nutrient-rich, protective structure
  — the plant's own developmental machinery, redirected for the
  insect's benefit
- Some caterpillars' saliva contains **effector molecules** (e.g.
  glucose oxidase) that actively **suppress** the plant's induced
  defense response while feeding — turning down the jasmonic-acid
  alarm from the inside
- Conceptually similar to how many plant pathogens use effector
  proteins to disable host immunity

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This is the most sophisticated countermeasure category -
not avoiding or neutralizing the defense, but disabling the plant's
own signaling before it fully activates.
:::

## The arms race continues

Every plant defense in this week's framework — physical, chemical,
constitutive, induced, even tolerance — has been met with a herbivore
counter-adaptation somewhere. Neither side "wins" permanently.

**This is exactly what happened with phylloxera and European
grapevines — except the vines had no counter-adaptation ready at
all. Coevolution takes time; introduce a novel enemy (or a novel
host) and that history simply isn't there yet.**

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min close. Full-circle callback to the opening story. Sets up
next week's indirect resistance as yet another layer in the same
ongoing arms race.
:::
